extracted.intended_audience: students, poets, playwrights, and critics studying poetic/dramatic theory (esp. tragedy and comedy)
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and evaluative standards for composing or analysing dramatic poetry (especially Greek tragedy and comedy): what a tragedy/comedy is, its necessary parts, and how to construct an effective plot, characters, diction, meter, and spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation (Mimesis) as the basis of poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry arises from the instinct of imitation; humans are the most imitative of animals and take pleasure in things imitated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imitation is natural and pleasurable because it enables learning and inference (we 'delight to contemplate' likenesses and learn from them). This underpins all poetic forms: poetry imitates actions, characters, and life. Examples/notes: even objects that cause pain can be pleasurable when accurately imitated; imitation plus rhythm/harmony yields poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instinct for harmony and rhythm
rubrics_metrics.description: Alongside imitation, humans have an instinct for harmony and rhythm; metres are sections of rhythm and contributed to the development of poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explains the origin and persistence of metrical forms; metre and musical elements are essential embellishments of poetic language and affect form selection (e.g., iambic as colloquial).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is an imitation of an action that is serious, complete, and of a certain magnitude; in embellished language; in the form of action, not narrative; through pity and fear effecting the proper purgation (catharsis) of these emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key parts must combine to produce catharsis. 'Language embellished' means rhythm, harmony, and song enter; some parts are rendered in verse alone, others with song. Tragedy imitates action (pragmata), not merely character or quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six constituent parts of Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Every Tragedy must have six parts: Plot (mythos), Character (ethos), Diction (lexis), Thought (dianoia), Spectacle (opsis), and Song (melopoeia).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two of these constitute the medium of imitation (song and diction), one the manner (thought), and three the objects (plot, character, spectacle). All plays contain these elements, but their relative importance differs (plot is chief).

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of Plot (Mythos)
rubrics_metrics.description: The plot is the imitation of the action (the arrangement of incidents) and is the most important element of tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A well-constructed plot is the soul of tragedy; it must be whole, unified, and causally coherent. Plots should contain peripeteia (reversal) and anagnorisis (recognition) where appropriate, and be crafted so incidents lead to one another by probability or necessity. Anti-pattern: a set of well-phrased speeches without a plot does not produce essential tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character (Ethos) as subsidiary to Plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Character is that in virtue of which we ascribe certain qualities to agents; it holds second place after plot and serves the actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Character should make clear the agents' dispositions and choices that produce acts, but action determines outcomes (happiness or reverse). A tragedy may lack detailed character portraiture yet still succeed if the plot (actions/incidents) is well composed. Example: Polygnotus vs Zeuxis analogy for painting vs style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought (Dianoia) — reasoning and thematic truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought is the faculty of saying what is possible and pertinent in given circumstances: proving, enunciating general truths, and apt argumentation in speeches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thought corresponds to the rhetorical/political function in oratory; it supplies the logical content and convincing statements within speeches. Use for delivering arguments, maxims, and revelations that advance the plot or clarify motives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction (Lexis) — expression in words
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction is the expression of the meaning in words; its essence is the same in verse and prose and includes metrical arrangement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diction includes choice of words, phrasing, and metrical construction ('the mere metrical arrangement of the words'). It must be appropriate to the form and capable of conveying thought and character. Novices often master diction before they can construct plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Song (Melopoeia) as an embellishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Song (melody) is a principal embellishment of tragedy and contributes strongly to its pleasurable elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Song enters in parts of the play where musical elements are appropriate; it is a chief source of delight but functions as decoration/enhancement of the action rather than the core structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectacle (Opsis) — visual/stage elements are least poetic
rubrics_metrics.description: Spectacle (scenic effect, props, stage machinery) has emotional attraction but is the least artistic part and the least connected with the poet's art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spectacle depends more on stagecraft and machinists than on the poet. The power of tragedy remains even without actual representation; thus do not rely on spectacle to substitute for poetic structure. The poet's craft lies primarily in plot, diction, and thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wholeness/Unity (Beginning, Middle, End)
rubrics_metrics.description: A whole is something with a beginning, a middle, and an end: the beginning does not itself follow anything by necessity, the end follows something and has nothing following it, and the middle follows and is followed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A properly constructed plot must neither begin nor end at haphazard points; the parts must be ordered so the whole forms a natural causal sequence. Use these definitions to judge completeness of structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnitude / Proper Length
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy must be of a certain magnitude: large enough to admit a complete action and changes (e.g., from good to bad fortune) yet not so large that the whole cannot be apprehended by the spectator's view or memory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beauty depends on magnitude and order; the proper magnitude allows the sequence to produce a reversal between fortune states. Too short makes events unmemorable; too long loses unity and perspicuity. Distinguish natural artistic limits from competition/time limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causal Coherence / Probability (Law of Probability or Necessity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Events in the plot ought to follow one another according to the law of probability or necessity; incidents should be causally connected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The plot's sequence should make transitions (e.g., from good fortune to bad) plausible or necessary. This causal necessity underpins the aesthetic and emotional impact (pity/fear). Anti-pattern: episodes linked only by coincidence or arbitrary concatenation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Peripeteia (Reversal) and Anagnorisis (Recognition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Peripeteia (reversal of the situation) and recognition scenes are powerful elements of emotional interest and are parts of the plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These devices intensify pity and fear and are central to producing catharsis. A well-timed reversal or recognition that arises naturally from the plot's causal chain is especially effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action over Character (Dramatic focus on deeds)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy imitates action, not men; life consists in action and its end is a mode of action. Character is secondary because actions determine fortunes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose plays emphasizing the arrangement and consequences of deeds. Anti-pattern: constructing drama primarily as a sequence of descriptive character portraits or speeches without meaningful causal action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity is not identity of hero
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity of plot does not consist in the unity of the hero; one man's many adventures do not necessarily form one action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume that because a single character's life is one person, all episodes of their life form a single artistic unity. Select and shape incidents into one coherent action (e.g., Homer excludes many of Odysseus's adventures to achieve unity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate metre/measure for genre and speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Different poetic forms require different metres: epic uses hexameters, iambic is 'most colloquial' and fits dialogue; measures changed historically (iambic replaced trochaic for certain dramatic uses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose metre appropriate to the form and tone: iambic suits conversational speech and dramatic dialogue; epic's single metre serves narrative form. Meter affects naturalness and perspicuity of diction/character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre distinctions: Comedy vs Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy imitates characters of a lower type and the ludicrous (a harmless ugliness), not necessarily full vice; its origin and history differ from tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic effect arises from something ugly but non-painful. Historical/structural notes: comedy derived from phallic songs and lampooning measures; comedy was long treated less seriously and has different conventions regarding chorus, masks, and prologues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution of modes within parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Some parts of a play are rendered by verse alone, others with the aid of song; the several kinds of artistic ornament should be found in separate parts of the play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designerially assign sections (what is sung vs what is recited) so that each part's mode fits its function (e.g., choral song versus spoken dialogue). Maintain appropriate balance of modes to preserve unity and effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perspicuity and apprehension by the audience
rubrics_metrics.description: The whole must be perspicuous so that the audience can easily embrace the sequence of events and the unity of the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure and magnitude should permit the spectator to apprehend the whole in one view/memory; avoid sprawling sequences that obscure causal links or overwhelm the audience's ability to follow the action.
